title: Health and enough
hookLine: health is the greatest gift, contentment the greatest wealth (Dhammapada 204)
tomorrow: why would a poem compare a good life to a tree?

cards: One side of the feed says hustle, the other says slow down, and both are selling something. Is wanting more a problem, or the point?
The Dhammapada's verse two hundred and four, in Max Müller's translation: "Health is the greatest of gifts, contentedness the best riches." Sounds settled.
But inside the Buddhist tradition, enough has two sides, and the story behind this verse starts at a royal dinner table.

teach.h: THE KING WHO ATE TOO MUCH.
teach.b: In the Samyutta Nikaya, King Pasenadi of Kosala has a habit: he eats huge meals. One day he comes to the Buddha straight from the table, heavy and huffing.
The Buddha offers a short verse: a person who is mindful and knows the measure in eating grows old slowly and keeps their life. The king has his nephew recite it at every meal.
Little by little he eats less, grows lighter, and one day, stroking his own limbs, says the Buddha has been kind to him twice over. View one, then: contentment.

teach.h: VIEW ONE: A BIRD WITH ONLY ITS WINGS.
teach.b: The Buddha praises a monk who is content with his robe and his bowl, carrying them the way a bird carries only its wings. Its best case: craving never fills, and enough is the only wealth no one can take. Now view two.
In another sutta the Buddha says he learned two things on his way to awakening: not to rest content with the good qualities he had, and not to give up striving.
Its best case: contentment can become an excuse, and the path asks you to keep going. Both are the Buddha's own words.
Some teachers put them together like this: be content with things, and never content with how far you've grown.
Bread and growth are different hungers, and the tradition keeps both views.

how: Buddhist monks and nuns keep few possessions and eat within set limits, practicing contentment (santutthi); teachers pair it with steady effort (viriya) in practice, so that contentment with things never becomes contentment with oneself.

o: eating only one small meal a day for health
giving away all your money to become pure
being satisfied with what you have, as true riches

games.q: two sides of enough: tap the pairs.
p: ate huge meals, then learned the measure
recited the verse at every meal
a monk content with robe and bowl
with the good qualities you have

s: Buddhism teaches never to want anything, even to grow
the Buddha said he did not rest content with the good qualities he had.
in the story, the king had the Buddha's verse recited at every meal
his nephew said it at each meal, and little by little he ate less.
contentment in the verse means settling for less in every part of life
teachers pair it: content with things, never content with your growth.

games.q: you lean toward view one: contentment is wealth. now state view two, 'don't rest content', at its strongest.
o: contentment can turn into an excuse; the path asks you to keep striving.
wanting more money and things is what drives a good life forward.
the verse about contentment was for kings, not for ordinary people.
games.why: view two's best case is the Buddha's own: he didn't rest content with his good qualities, and he didn't give up striving. both views are his.

practice: Rest one hand on your belly and breathe. Notice that each in-breath stops on its own when it's full; you don't have to force more in. Let that be enough, breath after breath.
If some part of you is hurting, rest the hand wherever it's comfortable instead.

wordCard.voice: Health and enough: the Dhammapada's greatest gift and best riches. Content with things, and still growing.

carryVoice: Your line: contentment is wealth, in what you have, not in who you've become. Ten days of verses, and the book closes for now.

sources.q: Health is the greatest of gifts, contentedness the best riches

sources.ref: Samyutta Nikaya 3.13, Donapaka Sutta (King Pasenadi's meals; the verse on knowing the measure; his nephew Sudassana recites it at each meal)
Digha Nikaya 2, Samannaphala Sutta (the monk content with robe and almsbowl, like a bird with its wings)
